regions.name: Frontal Lobe (Left)
regions.function: Executive control, working memory, voluntary motor planning, personality and impulse regulation, and expressive language (left side).
regions.clinical: Damage here produces disinhibition, apathy, poor judgment, or — if the inferior left portion is involved — expressive (Broca's) aphasia.

regions.name: Frontal Lobe (Right)
regions.function: Non-verbal executive function, sustained attention, and aspects of social/emotional judgment.
regions.clinical: Right frontal lesions are classically linked to disinhibition and impaired insight with relatively preserved language.

regions.name: Parietal Lobe (Left)
regions.function: Somatosensory integration, spatial processing, and (left side) mathematical reasoning and left-right orientation.
regions.clinical: Left angular gyrus damage can cause Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion.

regions.name: Parietal Lobe (Right)
regions.function: Spatial awareness of the whole body and surrounding space; attention allocation across both visual fields.
regions.clinical: Right posterior parietal lesions are the classic cause of hemispatial (left-sided) neglect.

regions.name: Temporal Lobe (Left)
regions.function: Auditory processing, semantic memory, and — in the posterior superior region — language comprehension.
regions.clinical: Posterior superior temporal damage on the left produces Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.

regions.name: Temporal Lobe (Right)
regions.function: Prosody (tone of speech), music perception, and facial/scene memory.
regions.clinical: Right temporal lesions can flatten prosody (aprosodia) and impair recognition of unfamiliar faces or environments.

regions.name: Occipital Lobe
regions.function: Primary and associative visual processing — edges, motion, color, and the start of the dorsal ('where') and ventral ('what') visual streams.
regions.clinical: Bilateral occipital infarcts (posterior cerebral artery) can cause cortical blindness; unilateral lesions cause contralateral visual field cuts.

regions.name: Cerebellum
regions.function: Coordination, balance, motor timing, and error-correction of movement; also contributes to cognitive timing and procedural learning.
regions.clinical: Lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia — never contralateral, unlike cortical motor lesions.

regions.name: Brainstem
regions.function: Midbrain, pons, and medulla — houses cranial nerve nuclei, and cardiorespiratory and arousal (reticular activating system) centers.
regions.clinical: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: crossed sensory loss, Horner's syndrome, dysphagia, and ataxia from PICA territory infarct.

regions.name: Broca's Area
regions.function: Speech production planning and grammatical (syntactic) construction of language, in the inferior frontal gyrus.
regions.clinical: Damage causes non-fluent, effortful, telegraphic speech with intact comprehension and impaired repetition — Broca's aphasia.

regions.name: Wernicke's Area
regions.function: Language comprehension — decoding the meaning of spoken and written words, at the posterior superior temporal gyrus.
regions.clinical: Damage causes fluent but meaningless ('word salad') speech, with impaired comprehension and impaired repetition — Wernicke's aphasia.

regions.name: Amygdala
regions.function: Fear conditioning, threat detection, and emotional tagging of memories. Normally bilateral; shown here on one side for clarity.
regions.clinical: Bilateral damage (e.g. Klüver–Bucy syndrome) causes placidity, hyperorality, and hypersexuality; also implicated in PTSD hyperactivity.

regions.name: Hippocampus
regions.function: Formation of new declarative (episodic and semantic) memories and spatial navigation. Normally bilateral.
regions.clinical: Bilateral medial temporal damage (e.g. patient H.M.) produces anterograde amnesia with preserved procedural learning.

regions.name: Thalamus
regions.function: The brain's major sensory relay station (except olfaction), routing signals to appropriate cortical areas; also involved in arousal.
regions.clinical: Thalamic stroke can cause central post-stroke pain syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy) — severe contralateral burning pain.

regions.name: Hypothalamus
regions.function: Homeostasis: temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythm, and control of the pituitary/endocrine axis.
regions.clinical: Lesions can cause diabetes insipidus, temperature dysregulation, or disrupted sleep-wake cycles.

regions.name: Corpus Callosum
regions.function: The largest white-matter tract, carrying information between the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
regions.clinical: Split-brain (callosotomy) patients show striking hemisphere-specific deficits, e.g. left-hand alien-limb-like behaviour.

regions.name: Primary Motor Cortex
regions.function: The precentral gyrus — the motor homunculus. Controls voluntary movement of the contralateral body, organized medial (leg) to lateral (face).
regions.clinical: Lesions cause contralateral spastic weakness; MCA territory infarcts spare the leg (supplied by ACA) but affect face/arm most.

regions.name: Primary Somatosensory Cortex
regions.function: The postcentral gyrus — receives touch, pressure, vibration, and proprioceptive input from the contralateral body.
regions.clinical: Lesions cause contralateral cortical sensory loss: impaired two-point discrimination and stereognosis with preserved crude touch.

regions.name: Insula
regions.function: Interoception (internal body awareness), taste, pain processing, and emotional awareness/disgust.
regions.clinical: Implicated in addiction (craving states) and in autonomic changes seen after right insular strokes.

regions.name: Basal Ganglia
regions.function: Caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus — action selection, procedural/habit learning, and movement modulation.
regions.clinical: Degeneration causes Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor) or Huntington's disease (chorea), depending on the circuit affected.
